title: Informal Fallacies in the Wild
subtitle: Why bad arguments feel good, and how to argue against the best version of your opponent
objectives: By the end you will be able to distinguish formal fallacies from informal fallacies and explain why informal fallacies depend on context.
By the end you will be able to identify ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, slippery slope and fallacious appeals to authority or popularity in real discourse.
By the end you will be able to explain when superficially similar moves (questioning a source's reliability, predicting consequences, deferring to experts) are perfectly reasonable.
By the end you will be able to describe motivated reasoning and explain why it makes fallacies so attractive.
By the end you will be able to construct a steelman of a view you reject.
hook:
Scroll through any comment section and you can play fallacy bingo. "You only say that because you're rich." "So you think we should just let criminals run wild?" "If we allow this, next thing you know..." "Ninety percent of people agree with me." Each line has a name, many of them Latin, and spotting them can feel like a superpower.

But there is a catch that most fallacy lists leave out. Every one of those moves has a legitimate cousin. Sometimes a speaker's interests really are relevant. Sometimes a policy really is a first step down a slope. Sometimes you should trust the experts. The skill this lesson teaches is not name-calling ("That's an ad hominem!") but judgment: telling when a move undermines an argument and when it does not. And it ends by turning the spotlight around, onto the reasoner most likely to fool you: yourself.

sections.heading: Formal and Informal Fallacies
sections.body:
In Lessons 1 and 2 you met **formal fallacies**, like affirming the consequent: arguments that are invalid because of their shape alone. You can catch them with a truth table or a countermodel, no matter what the argument is about.

An **informal fallacy** is different. It is a flaw in reasoning that cannot be detected from form alone; you have to look at the content, the context and the purpose of the argument. Many informal fallacies are not even invalid in the formal sense. "This newspaper is reliable, because it says so in this newspaper, and what this newspaper says is reliable" is valid (its conclusion is one of its premises), but it is useless as persuasion. This is **begging the question**, or circular reasoning: assuming what you are supposed to prove. (Note that in everyday English "begs the question" often means "raises the question," which is not the logician's sense.)

The study of fallacies goes back to Aristotle's *Sophistical Refutations*, a guide to the tricks used by the paid debaters you met on Day 8. Aristotle listed thirteen kinds of fallacious refutation, some based on language (like ambiguity, which he called **equivocation**) and some not. The Latin names (*ad hominem*, *ad populum*, *ad verecundiam*) mostly come later, many from early modern logic textbooks; John Locke used several of them in his *Essay* (1690).

In 1970 the Australian philosopher Charles Hamblin published *Fallacies*, a devastating critique of what he called the "standard treatment": textbooks defining a fallacy as an argument that seems valid but is not, and then listing examples that are not invalid at all, without explaining why they are bad. Hamblin's book launched a field, now called **argumentation theory** or informal logic, that studies arguments as moves in a dialogue. Its central insight, developed by Douglas Walton and others: whether a move is fallacious depends on the kind of conversation you are in and whether the move helps or derails it.

sections.heading: Attacking the Person: Ad Hominem and Its Legitimate Cousins
sections.body:
An **ad hominem** ("to the person") argument responds to a claim by attacking the person who makes it rather than the claim itself. It comes in several flavors:
- **Abusive**: "Don't listen to her theory of inflation; she's an idiot."
- **Circumstantial**: "Of course he says the factory is safe; he owns it."
- **Tu quoque** ("you too"): "You tell me to quit smoking, but you smoke!"

In each case, the conclusion that the claim is false does not follow. A smoker can give perfectly good reasons to quit; an owner might be telling the truth. Truth does not depend on the character of the person who states it.

But notice the important distinction between an **argument** and **testimony**. If someone gives you an argument, you can check the premises and the reasoning yourself, so their character is irrelevant. If someone asks you to believe something *on their word*, as a witness does, then their honesty, competence and interests are directly relevant. A court that let a jury hear that a witness was paid by the defendant would not be committing a fallacy. It would be assessing credibility.

So the circumstantial ad hominem is fallacious when used to *refute* a claim and legitimate when used to *discount testimony*. "He owns the factory, so his reassurance is not independent evidence; let's get an inspector" is good reasoning. "He owns the factory, so the factory is dangerous" is not.

A close relative is the **genetic fallacy**: judging an idea by its origin rather than its merits. Nietzsche's genealogy of morals (Day 65) is sometimes accused of this. Showing that a moral idea arose from resentment does not by itself show it is false, though, as Nietzsche's defenders point out, a debunking genealogy can legitimately weaken our confidence that we hold the belief *because* it is true.

sections.heading: Straw Men, Weak Men and the Art of Steelmanning
sections.body:
A **straw man** argument misrepresents an opponent's position, usually as something weaker or more extreme, and then knocks down the distortion. Politician A says: "We should spend less on the military." Politician B replies: "My opponent wants to leave our country defenseless." The name comes from the image of fighting a scarecrow instead of a real opponent: an easy victory over nobody.

A subtler cousin is sometimes called the **weak man** (or nut-picking): you accurately quote a real but unrepresentative defender of a view, the least thoughtful person on the other side, and treat refuting them as refuting the view. Social media is a weak-man factory, because the most extreme statements travel furthest.

The antidote is the **principle of charity**: interpret others' claims in their most reasonable sense before evaluating them. Its active form is **steelmanning**: building the strongest version of your opponent's argument, even stronger than they put it, and engaging with that. Daniel Dennett, in *Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking* (2013), popularized a set of rules he attributed to the game theorist Anatol Rapoport. Before criticizing someone's view, you should:
1. Re-express their position so clearly and fairly that they say, "Thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it that way."
2. List any points of agreement.
3. Mention anything you have learned from them.
4. Only then say a word of rebuttal or criticism.

There are three reasons to steelman. It is fair. It is more persuasive, because people stop listening once they feel misrepresented. And above all it protects you: if your view only survives against a straw man, you have not yet earned it. John Stuart Mill made this point in *On Liberty* (Day 62), as the quotation below shows.

A caution: steelmanning can be overdone. Sometimes a person really does hold the extreme view, and rewriting their claim into something sensible can let a bad argument off the hook. Charity means accurate interpretation, not wishful interpretation.

sections.heading: False Choices and Slippery Slopes
sections.body:
A **false dilemma** (or false dichotomy) presents two options as the only ones when others exist. "Either you support this bill or you don't care about children." "You're either with us or against us." In logical form it is a disjunctive syllogism (Lesson 1): P ∨ Q; ¬P; therefore Q. The form is valid. The problem is the first premise: the disjunction is false because it leaves out options R, S and T. That is why false dilemma is an informal fallacy: the flaw lies in content, not form.

Not every two-option choice is false. "Either the patient is pregnant or she isn't" exhausts the possibilities. The test is to ask: are these options really exhaustive, and really exclusive? Often a spectrum (how much military spending?) has been squashed into a binary.

A **slippery slope** argument claims that a first step will lead, through a chain of further steps, to a bad outcome, so we should not take the first step. "If we allow students to redo one test, soon they'll expect to redo every test, and grades will mean nothing."

Is this a fallacy? Sometimes. A slippery slope is a causal prediction, and like any prediction it can be well or poorly supported. Here is a useful way to assess one. Suppose the chain has four links, and each is fairly likely, say 70 percent. The probability that all four happen is 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7, about 24 percent. Long chains of individually plausible steps produce implausible destinations. The fallacy lies in presenting the far end of the slope as certain or highly probable without evidence for each link.

But some slopes are real. Legal precedents can genuinely make the next step easier; institutional "mission creep" is a documented phenomenon. Critics of a policy who point to specific mechanisms ("once the database exists, other agencies will request access, as happened in cases X and Y") are making a reasonable argument, not a fallacious one. A second kind, the *conceptual* slippery slope ("if one grain isn't a heap and adding one grain never makes a difference, then nothing is a heap"), is a genuine logical paradox, and you will meet it as the sorites in Lesson 5.

sections.heading: Authorities and Crowds
sections.body:
An **appeal to authority** (in Latin, *ad verecundiam*, roughly "to modesty" or "to respect") supports a claim by citing someone who believes it. Since nobody can check everything personally, most of what you know rests on trusted sources: doctors, textbooks, encyclopedias. Deferring to genuine expertise is not a fallacy; it is rational.

The appeal becomes fallacious when:
- The authority is not an expert *in this field*: a famous physicist's opinions on nutrition carry no special weight.
- Experts in the field substantially disagree, so citing one hides the controversy.
- The authority has a conflict of interest or is anonymous ("scientists say...").
- The claim is presented as true *because* the authority said it, closing off further evidence.

A useful checklist when someone cites an authority: Is this person an expert in the relevant domain? Is the claim within that expertise? Is there broad expert consensus? Is the source reported accurately? Is there evidence of bias?

The **appeal to popularity** (*ad populum*, or bandwagon) argues that a claim is true because many people believe it. Most people once believed the Sun orbits the Earth. On its own, popularity is weak evidence of truth. But it is not zero evidence in every case. If thousands of independent people report that a restaurant is good, that is information. The key word is *independent*: if the crowd's beliefs came from one shared source, or from imitating each other, their numbers add little. And in some domains, such as what words mean or which side of the road to drive on, what people generally do largely settles the matter.

sections.heading: The Enemy Within: Motivated Reasoning
sections.body:
Why do fallacies work? Partly because they exploit shortcuts that are usually useful. But a deeper reason is that we often reason toward conclusions we already want.

**Motivated reasoning** is the tendency to evaluate arguments and evidence in a way that favors a desired conclusion. The psychologist Ziva Kunda, in an influential 1990 review, argued that people do not simply believe whatever they want; they construct justifications that seem reasonable to them, while applying stricter standards to unwelcome evidence. Its cousin, **confirmation bias**, is the tendency to seek and remember evidence that supports what we already believe. Ask yourself whether you check a news story you like as carefully as one you dislike.

Research suggests that more intelligent or educated people are not immune. Some studies, such as those by Dan Kahan and colleagues on what he calls identity-protective cognition, have found that on politically charged topics, people with greater numerical skill can be *more* polarized, because they are better at finding reasons for the position their group holds. These findings are debated and some have not replicated cleanly, but the general warning stands: cleverness is a tool that can serve truth or serve self-defense.

The cognitive scientists Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber, in *The Enigma of Reason* (2017), offer an intriguing explanation. They argue that human reasoning evolved not mainly to find truth alone, but to produce arguments to persuade others and to evaluate others' arguments. On this view, we are lazy and biased when producing our own arguments but fairly sharp at spotting flaws in others'. That predicts that reasoning works best in groups that genuinely disagree and argue in good faith.

Here the threads of this lesson come together. Fallacy-spotting aimed only at opponents can become one more tool of motivated reasoning. The fallacy list is most valuable when turned on our own side, and steelmanning is valuable because it forces us out of the defensive crouch. Socrates (Day 9) would have recognized the project: the examined life begins with suspecting your own certainty.

keyQuote.text: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
keyQuote.source: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859), Chapter 2

modernConnection.title: Outrage Algorithms and the Straw Man Economy
modernConnection.body:
On social media platforms, what spreads is often what provokes. Studies of online sharing have repeatedly found that posts expressing moral outrage and hostility toward the other side tend to receive more engagement. A 2021 study by Steve Rathje and colleagues found that posts referring to political opponents were substantially more likely to be shared than posts about one's own side. Recommendation algorithms that optimize for engagement can amplify exactly these posts.

The result is an environment almost designed to manufacture straw men and weak men. If you only meet the other side through the most extreme clips, chosen because they make you angry, you will come to believe that opponents hold views far more extreme than most of them do. Political scientists call this a **perception gap**; surveys by the organization More in Common in the United States found that partisans substantially overestimate how extreme the other side's views are. False dilemmas thrive too: complex issues get flattened into two hashtags.

There is also a newer trap. Labeling things as fallacies has itself become a rhetorical weapon. Shouting "ad hominem!" or "slippery slope!" can be a way to dismiss a legitimate concern without engaging it. Philosophers call the mistake of concluding that a claim is false because someone argued for it badly the **fallacy fallacy**: a bad argument for a conclusion does not show that the conclusion is false.

What would good digital argument look like? Some platforms have experimented with features that encourage reading an article before sharing it, or that add community-written context to viral claims. These help, but the comparison with the classroom breaks down in an important way: philosophy seminars work because participants share a goal, finding the truth, while many online exchanges are performances for an audience. Steelmanning is hard when your audience rewards you for dunking. That is a reason to practice it deliberately, in places and with people where good faith is possible.

vocabulary.definition: A flaw in reasoning that depends on the content or context of an argument rather than its logical form.
vocabulary.example: A false dilemma can have a perfectly valid form yet rely on a false premise that hides other options.

vocabulary.definition: Responding to a claim by attacking the person making it instead of the claim or argument.
vocabulary.example: 'She's never held a job, so her economic argument is nonsense' is an ad hominem.

vocabulary.definition: Misrepresenting an opponent's position as weaker or more extreme than it is, then attacking that distortion.
vocabulary.example: Answering 'we should regulate social media' with 'so you want the government to censor everything' sets up a straw man.

vocabulary.definition: Reconstructing an opposing argument in its strongest possible form before evaluating it.
vocabulary.example: Before criticizing vegetarianism, she steelmanned it so well that her vegetarian friend asked to borrow her wording.

vocabulary.definition: Presenting two options as the only possibilities when others exist.
vocabulary.example: 'Either we cut all taxes or the economy collapses' is a false dilemma.

vocabulary.definition: Arguing that a first step will lead through a chain of consequences to an extreme outcome; fallacious when the links are unsupported.
vocabulary.example: Claiming that a four-day work week will inevitably end with nobody working at all is a weak slippery slope argument.

vocabulary.definition: Circular reasoning: assuming in the premises the very conclusion that is supposed to be proved.
vocabulary.example: 'He's trustworthy because he told me he never lies' begs the question.

vocabulary.definition: The tendency to evaluate evidence and arguments so as to reach a conclusion one already wants.
vocabulary.example: Fans who scrutinize every foul against their team but never fouls by it are engaged in motivated reasoning.

thinkingExercise.title: Steelman Your Opponent
thinkingExercise.prompt: Choose a contested issue on which you hold a firm view (for example, a political, ethical or lifestyle question). Your goal is to understand the other side well enough to pass Rapoport's first rule.
steps: Write down the worst version of the opposing view you have encountered. Name any fallacies it contains.
Now write the strongest version of the opposing view you can construct, in 150–200 words, including its best evidence and deepest values. Avoid any straw man or weak man.
List two points on which you agree with the steelmanned view and one thing you have learned from it.
Only now write your strongest objection to it. Check your objection for ad hominem, false dilemma, slippery slope or appeals to popularity.
Reflect: did your confidence in your own view change? Rate it from 1 to 10 before and after.

summary: Informal fallacies are flaws that depend on content and context rather than form; since Hamblin (1970), argumentation theorists judge them as moves that help or derail a dialogue.
Ad hominem attacks are fallacious as refutations but questioning a witness's credibility is legitimate when we rely on their testimony.
Straw men and weak men distort opponents; the principle of charity and steelmanning (Rapoport's rules) are the remedies.
False dilemmas hide options; slippery slopes are fallacious when the links are unsupported, but some causal slopes are real and long chains of probabilities shrink quickly.
Appeals to genuine, relevant, consensus expertise are rational; appeals to popularity are weak unless the crowd is independent.
Motivated reasoning and confirmation bias make fallacies attractive, so the best use of fallacy-spotting is on our own arguments.

quiz.question: What distinguishes an informal fallacy from a formal one?
options: Informal fallacies cannot be detected from logical form alone; content and context matter
Informal fallacies only occur in spoken argument
quiz.explanation: Formal fallacies are invalid by form. Informal fallacies require looking at what is said and in what context; some are even formally valid, like begging the question.

quiz.question: A jury hears that a key witness was paid by the defendant. Considering this is:
quiz.explanation: When we rely on someone's word, their interests and reliability are relevant. Ad hominem is fallacious when it is used to refute an argument we could assess on its own merits.

quiz.question: Steelmanning means presenting an opponent's argument in its strongest form before criticizing it.
quiz.explanation: Steelmanning is the opposite of a straw man: you build the best version of the view, sometimes better than its defenders do.

quiz.question: 'Either we ban cars from the city center or we accept that our children will breathe toxic air forever.' The main problem is:
options: A false dilemma that ignores options such as low-emission zones
quiz.explanation: The argument presents two options as exhaustive when there are many intermediate policies. Its form (disjunctive syllogism) is valid; the disjunctive premise is false.

quiz.question: A slippery slope argument has five steps, each with an estimated 80% chance of following from the last. Roughly how likely is the final outcome?
quiz.explanation: 0.8 multiplied by itself five times is about 0.33. Chains of individually likely steps can end in fairly unlikely outcomes.

quiz.question: Any appeal to authority is a fallacy, since a claim's truth does not depend on who believes it.
quiz.explanation: Deferring to genuine, relevant experts with broad consensus is rational. The appeal is fallacious when the authority is outside their field, disputed, biased, or used to shut down evidence.

quiz.question: Which best describes the 'weak man' tactic?
options: Quoting a real but unrepresentative, poorly reasoned defender of a view and treating their failure as the view's failure
Refusing to argue with a weak opponent
quiz.explanation: Unlike the straw man, the weak man is a real person accurately quoted, but they are the least capable representative of the position.

quiz.question: According to Mercier and Sperber's argumentative theory of reasoning, human reasoning:
options: Evolved to find truth through solitary reflection
Is free of bias in experts
Evolved largely to persuade others and evaluate their arguments, working best in groups that disagree
quiz.explanation: They argue we are biased in producing our own arguments but good at critiquing others', so honest group debate is where reasoning shines.

quiz.question: If someone defends a conclusion with a fallacious argument, the conclusion must be false.
quiz.explanation: This inference is itself the 'fallacy fallacy'. A bad argument fails to support its conclusion, but the conclusion may still be true for other reasons.

goDeeper.body:
After Hamblin, two major schools reshaped the study of fallacies. The **pragma-dialectical** approach of Frans van Eemeren and Rob Grootendorst at the University of Amsterdam treats an argument as an attempt to resolve a difference of opinion and lays down rules for a critical discussion: for example, that parties must not prevent each other from advancing standpoints, and that an attack must relate to the standpoint actually advanced. On this view, every fallacy is a violation of one of these rules. An ad hominem violates the freedom rule (it tries to silence a party rather than test their view); a straw man violates the standpoint rule.

Douglas Walton developed a related theory based on **argumentation schemes**: recurring patterns of presumptive reasoning, like "argument from expert opinion" or "argument from consequences," each with its own list of **critical questions**. A scheme is not deductively valid; it shifts the burden of proof. An argument from expert opinion is reasonable until someone raises a critical question it cannot answer (Is the expert biased? Do other experts agree?). A fallacy, for Walton, is a scheme used in a way that blocks the critical questions. This framework has proven useful in artificial intelligence and law, where researchers build computer models of argumentation.

A third line of work comes from Bayesian epistemology. Ulrike Hahn and Mike Oaksford have argued that many classic fallacies are best analyzed probabilistically: arguments from ignorance ("there's no evidence the drug is harmful, so it's safe") can be strong or weak depending on how thoroughly we searched. This explains why the same form can be good in one case and bad in another, the puzzle Hamblin first raised.

readings.author: Douglas Walton

questions: Is there a duty to steelman? Are there views so harmful or so obviously wrong that charity toward them would be a mistake?
If motivated reasoning affects everyone, how can we ever be confident that our own judgment of which arguments are fallacious is not itself motivated?
